title: Role registry
description: Governs content/competence/roles/registry.yaml. These are REFERENCE roles, not prescriptions. Roles are data, never code: an organization may edit, delete, add, or entirely replace this set through its local overlay without touching the corpus, and its own job titles will drive gap analysis exactly as the shipped ones do. The shipped set exists so the platform is useful on first run, not because these are the correct roles for anyone in particular.

roleType.description:
WHAT KIND OF THING THIS ROLE IS, and the answer to a conflation the registry made for a while by listing two different kinds of thing side by side.

`occupational` — a job. It has a competence profile of its own, and a person's gaps against it are gaps in what they are expected to be able to do.

`authority-overlay` — a permission an organization grants, carried ON TOP of an occupational role. A person is *Calibration Engineer AND Approved Signatory*; the signatory authority does not describe their occupational competence, it describes what they are permitted to do. `approved-signatory` sat beside `calibration-engineer` and `laboratory-manager` as though it were the same kind of thing, and the consequence was concrete: gap analysis reported 'short of L3 for approved-signatory' as a COMPETENCE gap, so an organization could read closing those gaps as the route to signatory status. It is not. The authority is granted, recorded in an authorization, and ends when the person leaves — see rule 6 and authorization.schema.json. That is exactly the collapse the dual-object model exists to prevent, reappearing in the role model.

An overlay still carries roleTargets, and they still mean something real: the competence the authority PRESUPPOSES. 'Is this person competent to be granted this?' is a legitimate question and the targets answer it. What they never answer is 'has this person earned this?', because nobody earns an authority.

A deployment scope names an occupational role in `role` and any overlays in `overlays`; the validator rejects an overlay in `role`, because a scope whose only role is an overlay produces precisely the misreading above.

REQUIRED rather than defaulted. An organization replacing this registry with its own job titles has to classify each one, and being made to decide is the point — the distinction is invisible until somebody is told it exists.

family.description: Broad grouping used for dashboard rollups and for suggesting adjacent career paths. A role belongs to exactly one family; cross-family movement is normal and is precisely what the gap analysis is meant to illuminate.

summary.description: What the role actually does day to day, and what distinguishes it from its neighbours. Vague summaries produce meaningless role targets.

seniority.description: Relative ordering hint within a family, used only for display. Deliberately not a hierarchy of worth — an Approved Signatory and a Principal Metrologist are not comparable on one axis.

typicalScope.description: The breadth of responsibility typical for the role: single instrument, discipline, laboratory, site, enterprise, national.

authorities.description: Formal authorities the role commonly carries — approving calibration certificates, acting as an approved signatory, conducting assessments. Recorded because authority and knowledge are different things: a person may understand a method thoroughly and still not be authorised to sign for it.
